reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: A congenital deformity present at birth in which the foot is held in equinus, hindfoot varus, midfoot cavus, and forefoot adductus (remembered as the components of talipes equinovarus)
The key clinical distinction is between a rigid, structural clubfoot and a flexible 'postural' foot that corrects with gentle manipulation
It is often idiopathic but may be associated with neuromuscular conditions (e.g. spina bifida), syndromes, or oligohydramnios, so a general and neurological examination is important
Diagnosis is clinical; the deformity is frequently detected on antenatal ultrasound, and examination should exclude associated abnormalities such as developmental dysplasia of the hip
The Ponseti method of serial casting is the mainstay of treatment, gradually correcting the deformity, usually followed by a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy to address residual equinus
Maintenance with a foot-abduction (boots-and-bar) orthosis is essential to prevent relapse, and poor brace compliance is the commonest cause of recurrence
Treatment should begin early in the neonatal period when the tissues are most amenable to correction
Surgery is reserved for resistant, relapsed, or neglected deformities not corrected by casting
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital talipes equinovarus arises from abnormal development and positioning of the bones, joints, muscles, and soft tissues of the foot and ankle, with contracture of the medial and posterior soft tissues (including the tendo Achillis, tibialis posterior, and plantar structures) and abnormal alignment of the talus, calcaneus, and navicular. The exact cause is multifactorial, with genetic predisposition and intrauterine factors implicated; in syndromic or neuromuscular cases an underlying disorder disturbs the muscle balance across the developing foot. The result is a fixed deformity combining hindfoot equinus and varus with midfoot cavus and forefoot adduction, which becomes increasingly rigid and structurally established if untreated.
additionalDifferentials: Postural (positional) talipes that corrects fully with manipulation
Neuromuscular clubfoot (e.g. secondary to spina bifida or arthrogryposis)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination to assess rigidity and classify severity
Full musculoskeletal and neurological examination to detect associated conditions
Examination and, if indicated, imaging of the hips for developmental dysplasia
Antenatal ultrasound detection and postnatal confirmation
Spinal imaging or specialist assessment where a neuromuscular cause is suspected
redFlags: Associated neuromuscular disorder or spinal dysraphism requiring broader assessment
Failure to progress with casting, or early relapse, indicating a resistant or syndromic foot
Neglected or late-presenting rigid deformity limiting non-surgical correction
Signs of an alternative diagnosis such as congenital vertical talus
reference.prognosis: With early Ponseti treatment and disciplined brace use, most idiopathic clubfeet achieve a functional, plantigrade, pain-free foot, though a minority relapse and need repeat casting or surgery; syndromic and neuromuscular clubfeet are stiffer, more prone to recurrence, and have a less predictable outcome.
pitfalls: Mistaking a rigid structural clubfoot for a flexible postural foot and delaying treatment
Under-emphasising brace compliance, the leading cause of relapse
Overlooking an associated neuromuscular or syndromic condition, or concurrent hip dysplasia
Attempting forceful correction or premature surgery instead of graduated casting
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Ponseti serial manipulation and casting is the mainstay, progressively correcting the cavus, adductus, varus and equinus components of the deformity.
Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy to correct residual hindfoot equinus at the end of casting.
Maintenance in a foot-abduction (boots-and-bar) orthosis to prevent relapse, with intensive parental education since poor brace compliance is the commonest cause of recurrence.
Assessment for and management of associated conditions such as developmental dysplasia of the hip and neuromuscular disorders.
Surgery for relapsed, resistant or syndromic feet, including tibialis anterior tendon transfer or posteromedial soft-tissue release.
Long-term orthopaedic follow-up to detect and treat recurrence through skeletal growth.
